..... Warringt,n has some claim to having published tlt. first newspaper in Lancashire. This was . . ,
" Erre's WeeklijMarina, or Warrington Adverrift,r,- 1, he tlr4 number of which W. ismed from the press ! of Thomaa and William Eyr,..s oh Tomiday, the 23rd of March, 17.11 i.

The woodcut which embellished the top of the front page of this oil newspaper will be found to have a good deal of local interest. It represents ' t lie pot-boy of the period riding out of the town to the south, over the old stone bridge which then , spanned the Mersey at Warrington, and it is said to be the only representation extant in which the watch-house on the first pier of the bridge was given. This block, it may be mentioned, is still I preserved in our local Museum.

The William Eyres, motioned above, was a notable man in some respects, and Mr. Kendrick, in his " Warrington Warbles," says Ito was one of the list printers of his day, not even excepting those of the metropolis. As specimens of the beau- tiful typography whirl, issued from the Warring- ton press, whilst antler his management, we have Dr. Aikin's "Translation of the Life of Agricola, by Tacitus, 1774' ; the two memorable books of the great philanthropist. Howard, on the "State of Prisons in England,- and on "Lazarettos." Wat- son's "History of the House of Warren,- also printed by Mr. Eyres, wao designated by Gilbert Wakefield as "perhaps the most accurate specimen of typography ever produced by any press." --- Mr. Eyres wasn't, however, commended for every- thing he did in the printing line. Mr. J. Fitchett Marsh, in his "Literary Ili-tory of Warrington." says that "infamous book "—Mr. Marsh was clearly a strong Tory—" The Age of ite144011." written by the " " Thomas Paine, woo pnnted by Mr. Gyres. who, to escape detection, set up the type and printed off the copies with his own hands in the night, after his workmen haul left the printing office.
Mr. Eyres was born at Warrington in 1734; he , was colonel of the local volantecrs in 1,404; and he died at Warrington. September 14, POI.

Another of the earlier Warrington periodical pub- lications was "The Butterfly," a "series of literary papers to be continued weekly." It was first pubs fished on December 31, W.ri, by .1. Crowther, of Bridges:4. From the only item of benl news which appeared in the tirst nmnber, 1 gather that there I was a complaint then as now that high-class music , was not over well patronim,l. There had been a concert in the town and very badly attended, though it W{l,l declared to be so far" above mediocrity" that It" would not have disgraced the metropolis."

“The Battorfle” inereaPel in size and in price. When first published it consisted of four pages of ordinary pamphlet size. and twopence was charged for it. On April Cl. 1c27. there were I metre pages for which the reader hail to pay sixpence.

Editors were criticised in those data as well as ecit eat. TOO editor of "The Butterfly" ackoow- . ledges a commonication from a lady correspondent. relative to the " deficiency of anecdote and scandal I in his paper, and this is how Ito" rose to the oven- : slow" "We have, he says,' taken the moat eels MOOAlitOff to remedy the evil. We have scoats every post-house and hamlet within ten mil,s f, the purpose of gleaning every passing occurrence, from a fractured horse-shoe toe cracked repeat ion ; and oar reporter at Padgate Stocks ha- just sent On in a Inalaet of which, but for the pressure of !nisi- nem, we should have availed ourselves."

There MIS another journalistic enterprise in War- rington which met with a very scanty success. This was a "Warrington Observer," a weekly journal of " literary, religions and miscellaneous information " the first number of which appeared on Wednesday. June 2nd, Mal It was a small four- paged paper, and sold at three-pence.

The "Observer" slid not flourish, tor efind that on the 21st July—six or seven weeks from its com- mencement -the editor complains that the sale was not more than 130 copies a week, which barely paid for Isbnitr, to say not 111,12 01 the consumption of lower," ware awl taro" "Cater these cir- ' cumstances,deeply and well considered,' he can- didly confesses, "we are under the neces,ity of dis- continuing the paper until placed upon a different basis, not entirely upon our own responsibility."

Looking through these old Meg, I find that there I wat, a procession in Warrington on the 19th July, NW, the day when William IV was proclaimed king throughout the country. About eleven in the morning the procession was foravvl at tit.. Sessions House and moved through the principal streets of the tnwn in the following order Trumpeter on boraeback two staffmen; the Warrington band in military costume, new for the occaxion ; John Pitchett, Esq., came nest, supported on the right by the high constable and on the left by the deputy con- stable, all on horseback ; then the four chosen con- stables for the year on horseback ; a large silk flag ; magistrates and clergy and a number of respect- able inhabitants, the rear of all being brought up by Mr. Newsham and Mr. T. Litton on horseback. The proclamation was read by Mr. Fitchett.

On Monday evening, a meeting that had been organised by Mr. Paul, of the Anti-Tobacco League, Manchester, was held in Wycliffe Infant School. It Was annottnced that a lecture would be given by Or. Martin, formerly of Warrington, and now of Manchester. There was a good at.entlance, and the chair Wan occupied by Mr. John Walker. In open- ing the proceedings, the Uhair•nan said that there was no question that the practice of smoking Was ,on the IMMO+e. Some prattle nasals,' to get com- fort ant pleasure from it. They should get all the pleasure Put of life they conbl, hut at the same time it was a fair question to consider whether they might not have to pay too high a price for it. Medi- cal men recogaied now what was called " heart," just as they recognised " gin-drinkers' liver," and there was a growing opinion that cancer in the throat and tongue was due, in a large measure, to excessive smoking. In support of this statement he mentioned the fatal cases of General Grant and the Into Emperor Frederick lie then introduced Dr. Martin to the meeting, saying that he knew he might count on A warm welcome from a Warrington audience. (Applause.) Dr. Martin commenced be also n herring to General Grant and the Emperor Frederick. Ile ssid that they were 1111tilleg'ionably powerful men, and there could be hardly any doubt that the cancerous disease that bad ultimately proved fatal had been I,nflight on by both of them being great smokers. He detailed instances from his experience son °lndicai practitioner of the injurious, and even fatal, effect that had ultimately resulted from i the habit of smoking, and he dwelt, too, on the fart that l smoking had a tendency to make people exceedingly rel- I fish and inconsiderate of other people. The sick, ewes rially bronchial subjects, were often made worse by the fact that they had to live i,,a corn where members of the family indulged in the" weed." 114, then proceeded to refer tia the striatum and functions of the body, and dwelt upon the absolute necessity for securing largo quantities of fresh air as a means to the maintenance of sound health both of body and mind. Mr. Diegle followwl with one of lila characteris- tic speeches. He described the bad effect eta certain smoke, and said that he had never smoked since, although it was over fifty years ago. He had been an abstainer fir over twenty year, ' and now, although in his 78th year, le, was in good health,. Is reply to optestions, Or. Martin said that then, was no doubt as to the ill effects of smoking, and that ' deterioration might I7e going on almost unperceived, just as it did before the development of ealieer. div.head: BARNUM'S SHOW IN LONDON.
div.p: BARNUM'S SHOW IN LONDON.

Barnum's great international emporium of natur- al and artistic wonders was opened at Olympia on Monday night. The interior of the building has been entirely altered, and accommodation is now I provided for upwanls of 12.000 spectators, or ! 5.600 more than Olympia has ever contnined before. : Kondoners ere simply mad to sir the " greatest ! show in the world," and consequently every ! able seat was occupied long before the entertain_ ment commenced, and thousands of people who had taken trains to South Kensington were obliged , tin ret ern !mine disappointed. Tine show is really ' great, but like all great things it has its faults. There is too much of everything, and novelities are not abundant. If one milli! imagine three first- class enemies and two wild beast shows amalgam- ated going on at the same lime a pretty accurate idea of" the greatest show on earth "in gained. In theorems three circus rings have been constructed, and between the rings are two plat forms, on whieli acrobatic and other performances are given attire same time as the equestrian feats of the circles. oo that there an, II ve performances going on sim- ultaneously. Most of the feats and the greater part of the entertainments Sr.' excellent, but the spectto ors are simply bewildered, the chniee of entertainment being too great for the quickest-sighted people to see in one night. From the opening to the close the arena in full of life -at one tune strike charmers, performing camels, seals, Algerian bulls ;at another marvelloimly taught trick stallions, " clown " bears, Shetland ponies, and trick dogs then athletes and clowns looping over ele- Omits, giving most langhable and wildly absurd illustrations of comical agility, intrepid, bareback, hurdle acts, then some wonderful performances by la herd of elephants, and at another time n host of I gymnasts, acrobats, and trapezists. Nearly the I whole of the space on the west side of the building lis occupied by a huge panorama, repre,:enting ! Rome in the days of Nero. In front of this is per- , formed the romantic spectacle in live tablealix e Nero. or the destruction of Brune.' On this !spectacle Mr. Barnum has lavished the resources of Inns great establishment. On Monday night he ' succeeded in presenting a picture which in brilli- ancy, vastness, and variety windd astonish Nero himself if he molt only he persuaded to revisit the glimpses of the moon, as seen at the great building in South Kensington. In addition to the show in , the arena there is a wonderful collection of lions, , tigers, bears, wolves, hippopotamuses, elks, camels, and every other kind of animal known at the Zoological Gardens.

div.p: STANLEY'S RETURN TO ZANZIBAR.

Authentic new! has been received in Zanzibar that 'Mr H. M. Stanley haa written to Mr. Portal, saying that he hopes to be at Zanzibar about the middle of January. The explorer Flays nothing, however, about the route by which he will return.

The "Berliner[Rent. Nachrichten" states that 10 : days age Captain Wissman telegraphed to Berlin Boverninent informing them that Emin Pasha and Mr. Stanley were only 30 days march from 31pwapera, which lies inland about 200 iniles from the coast town of liagarnono. Captain Missman ha sent them provisions from Bagamoys. _

div.head: CLAYTON EXPLOSION. .ELEVENTH DEATH.
div.p: THE CLAYTON EXPLOSION. .ELEVENTH DEATH.

The death list in connedion with the dreadful explo- sion at the works of the Clayton Foundry Company, Limited, Clayton. on the 28th ,d last month, has been further extended. Alfred Hy. 38, of Collins-yard, Gnat Newton-A., Newton Hea• ii, who was burned about , the faca, arms, and thighs. died from exhaustion at the Royal Infirmary, at twelve minutes past eleven, on Sunday night. This makes the tenth death. One man I was killed on the spot, another died at the Ancoats fibs- Inst. and eight out of thirteen removed to the Infirmary have abio died from their terrible injuries. Hyde`ki death will necessitate another inquiry by the deputy city coroner. The eleventh sufferer who has succumbed to his injuries a Williain Travis, aged twenty-five, of Parker-st . Bradford. He was badly burned about the body erysipelas supeisened, and he died at Monssil Hospital.

F GREAT GLOVE FIGHT FOR 1:1,1,.,u0. At an early hour on NUin lay morning the great glove fight between Jam, Smith. champion of England, and Peter Jackson, champion f Australia, was disidod at the Pelican club, in Shaftesbury Avenue. The RUM of £l,OOO was tube divided, the winner taking £BOO and the loser £2OO. The date of the consist was kept a secret fora considerable Siam, but on Saturday and Sun- day night it toprame known in sporting circles generally. The first round was somewhat skive. Jackson boxing very skilfully. In the second round Jackson warmed up, fought Smith on to the ropes,. and kept him there, ham- mering away at him unrnermfully. Smith grew weak, and then rushing at Jackson threw hint. There woo at once a tremendous uproar in the I,OT, and when quiet had born motored the referee awarded the tight to liackson. The decision was based on Smith's violation of the Queensberry rules in throwing Jackson.

div.head: poLITICAL SPEECHES.
div.p: poLITICAL SPEECHES.

SIR. W. HARCOURT IN SUSSEX. Sir William Harcourt, speaking at a Liberal demon- stration at Stratford, iin Tue.lay night, said the sup- porters of the Government even expressed disappoint- ment with Lord Salisbury's speech at the Guildhalt. Referring to the recent by-elections, he contended that figures showed they had gime against the Government. The great national party was now washing its dirty linen at Birmingham, and was squabbling over the great national compact . The unitod Unionists were quarreling over the disposition of seats which they had not at their command. Gentlemen who would not remain in public life but for love of country were ready to fling the Union to the winds if necessary, and to become wicked Sepandists themselvos. The Tories were, however, beginning to get tired of the geme, and Mr. Chamber- laidtdictatorial style had made even Birmingham revolt, and they were beginning to ask why unionism should ! be made a stalking horse Inc the gratification of personal ! ambition and self-seeking manduvres. Mn. BALFOUR AT IPSWICH.

At Ipswich, on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Balfour was presented with a number of addresses from Conservative Indies in Suffolk, Norfolk, Lincolnshire, Cambridgeshire, and Essex. In reply, he said they did root doubt the o superiority of their cause to that of their opponents, but Ihe wished their organi.ation was aiso better. If they were prepared, he for one did not 17 herish the faintest doubt that at the next general election they would be entirely successful. Speaking in the evening, Mr. Bal- four clainusl that the Government had only used the Crimes Act to put down illegal combinations and the improvement in the condition of Ireland was due to the courageous policy of the Government. Ile denied that priests in Ireland had contributed in any material degivo I to the improvement, and as to Irish representatives, he I quoted Mr. Gladstone's expression that crime dogged the I footsteps of the League. A resolution of confidence in I the Government was named. .......

Liberals asked for the is iontry's confidence not merely , on the Irish question, but as being the most faithful interpreters of the wishes of the nation in matters of j domestic legislation. With regard to their programme, I they would he fools if they disclosed their plaits to opponents win, Loki tnem that they meant to remain in power for throe years longer, but there IVas a very wide ! range of subjects from which they could iihone. Among them were the large groupil questions affeeting working- urn—which would have to be dealt with quickly and thor:oughly by the next Liberal Government —the tablishment 1 the Church in Scotland and WaleS, the rmulation of the liquor traffic, mgis ration, and various , taller matters.

div.head: SHIP CANAL FOR SCOTLAND.
div.p: A SHIP CANAL FOR SCOTLAND.

IThe proposal to construct a ship canal to conneet the Forth and the Clyde is now being seriously taken up. Two routes have been suggested—one direct and the other by way of Loch Lomond. For the former the estimated cost is five millions, and for the latter—which has the support of Mr. E. Leader Williams, chief engineer of the Manchester Ship Canal—eight millions. In a report just prepared. Mr. Williams dwells strongly upon theimportance of mich a canal as that proposed. both for commercial purposes and from a national point of view in case of war. As to the nature of the work to be undertaken, Isi does not suppose that it will present any insuperable engineering diffieultim, awl he expects to find that, with the exception of locks at the entrances, the canal can be constructed with one level wateriline 1 throughout. If. considers, however, that details, ! surveys, and borings must be made before a definite ! course for the canal can be fully determined.

div.head: RAILWAY RATF.S.
div.p: RAILWAY RATF.S.

Mr. Findlay, general manager of the lamil,/n and North-Western Railway, was further crass-examined at ; the railway rates inquiry on Wednesday. Fle said he honestly believed that when the inaximuin rates were settled and the classification remrslelled there would be no material alteration of rates so faros the railway com- panies were concerned, unless some of the =tabours rates were made very much lower than the companies proposed. The interests of the companios and the traders were mutual, and Use ileifire of the companies was to encourage trade. If Parliament were to begin to fix the actual rates, the railways would have to become State railways. The inquiry will be resumed this ,

ittleadjourned inquiry, on Thursday, before the .ard of Trade, the general inanager of the London and NerthAVestern Railway admitted that during: the prevalence of high prices in 1873-4 the railway rates wens increased, and although those prices had dropped, the rates had probably not been reduced.—Questions I were put to Mr. Findlay by the representatives of the Wolverhampton Chamber of Commerce, the Chemical Manure Manufacturers' Association, and the traders os the Monmouthshire Railway.

div.head: ARRAN MURDER. LA(7RIE SENTENCED.
div.p: THE ARRAN MURDER. LA(7RIE SENTENCED.

The trial of John Watson Laurie for the murder of Edwin Rose, a tourist, in the island of Arran, in July last, was concluded at Edinburgh, before the Lord Chief Justice Clerk, on Saturday. Further evidence having been given for the persecution, three medical gentlemen of Edinburgh were called in support of the theory of the defence, that the injuries on the head and shoulder of Wee were the result of an accidental fall. The jury de- liberated for 40 minutes, awl then returned into court with the announcement that by a majority the prisoner Ihad keen found guilty. Sentexce of death was then passed. Laurie, who stood unmoved while his doom AVM being pronounced, d,ylared his innocence. The trial bastert until late in the evening. The enurt throughout I the day wale filled with eager listeners, and its precincts ! were thronged by an excited CrOWII. The execution was I fixed to take place at tirerteark, on November 30. I A petition for the repnere of Laurie, sentenced to I death for the Arran moose, has been started at OW- bridge. The chief plea is !hat seven of the fifteen jury- men voted for a verdict of not proven.

WINWICE-ST. OWITILUCTIONS. At the Warrington Borough Court, on Saturday, the case of the Corporation V. Gregg was mentioned, and it was decided to adjourn the hearing till the' 2.'3rd inst. It is a case in which John Gregg. brolier, Winwick-road. was summoned for having caused an obstruction in Winwick-road by allowing a quantity of goods to remain vn the footpath in front of hie premises. The chief Constable remarked that it was time the obstruction woo discontinued. No longer since than the previous evening there were two cart loads of furniture standing out of doors.— Mr. Browne, who appeared for the defendant, said it was in a corner where there could not be any obstruction whatever.--The Chief Constable said there was an obstruction, and he believed he had power to arrest the defendant if he persisted in defying the law, after the law had decided that obstruction should not take place. Ile would not say that he wouldn't take that step. Ile would take the responsibility of it if they persisted in the obstruction.

Prosecutor was a man of respectable appearance. and he said he was a painter by trade. Ile was married, but on Friday afternoon he was drinking with the urisonere at the Royal Arms and afterwards at t lie White Bear. Whilst at the last- named public-house the prisoner 'Nekton put her hand into one of his trousers pockets and took out six shillings. He subeequently gave information to the police. The charge against Burke was with- drawn, and she was called as a witness. She stated . that at the White Boar she saw Hodson take Is. 2d. from the prosecutor's pocket and place it on the seat. Taylor afterwards potting it into her pocket. The Chairman remarked that this made Taylor's Sib and Hodson's :30th appearance at that court. Hodson had only left gaol on the Friday morning. div.p: WARRINGTON eNITED IItADES COUNCIL.

The usual monthly meeting of this Council was held on Tuesday. After the transaction of routine Itusiness.the Secretary stated. in reply to a delegate. that the memorial with regard to the aslicart and van men in the employ of the Corporation had been preented to the chairman and members of the Sanitary Committee, and that a deputation from the Trade Council thy invitation of the Town Clerk) I had waited upon the Sanitary Committee and advocated the rights of the men to he allowed their dinner hour like other workingmen. The Chairman of the Cominittee (Alderman 'Sorg,...), and other members of the Committee, sympathised with the object the &mu- tation had in view, and promised to try and and out some system to carry on the work, in order to grant the request of the men. The Committee altos promised tone° the det utation again, but no communication had been I received up to the time of that meeting. The Secretary I was requested to write again to the Sanitary Committee, ! in order to ascertain if anything had how:lone to remove ! the grievance which existed, and was considered a din., grace to the town, repugnant to decency and cleanliness. The following is a copy of the nsenfirrial referred tn. "TO the chairman, and members of the Sanitary Committee of the Warrington Town Council.—Gentleinen.—We ven- ture to approach you upon a question the Trades Council think of importance, vis. : that, having had under eon- , ilderation for some thee pant the grievance o' the men I employed with the vans and ash carts in not having a specified tins, in which to get their dinner, and haying to I work continually throughout the day, wrote of opinion that there is a justification iii prysenting this memorial Ito you for your favourable consideration, and asking you, if practicable, to allow a dinner hour to the men so employed. An other employ.o under the Corporation can have their mid-day meal-time alloworl, certainly we , venture to think these inon are jUAtifieli in asking for the same privilege, and your petitioners (representing over 900 Trades ruionists of Warrington) trusts you will see I your way clear to grant our reAsonable request, and earn the respect of the public generally of Warrington."

div.head: VICAR OF ST. BARNABAS% WARRINGTON. AND HIS PARISHIONER.
div.p: THE VICAR OF ST. BARNABAS% WARRINGTON. AND HIS PARISHIONER.

Last evening a meeting in St. ibirnabas' vestry was brought to an untimely conclusion. Circulars I had been sent out liv the Vicar. the Rev. G. Allton, I to a small number of parishioners, earnestly re- I questing their attendance at a meeting ot the e Chnrch Committee," last evening. A number of other parishioners, including the people's warden, who allege that there is no such hotly as a " Church Committee," bearing of the meeting, turned up at the vestry. On their entering, the Vicar, who was 111.././I.llt with two oh her pemons (one of whom , was the church-keeper) declared that they were intruding upon a -devotional ' meeting of Sunday school teachers. Mr. Smith, the people's warden. expremeil the opinion that he had aright to attend any meeting in the vestry, but this Mr. Allton denied. The vestry, he said, was the Vicar's free- : hold, and the churchwarden had no right there.' even on /1 Sunday. t swept with his consent, lie protested against a devotional gathering being din- tuehn',i in that way, declared the meeting ad- journed x;ote elis, and ordered the church-keeper to put the gas out. This last order was carried out, and those present. finding thon=elves in darkness, left the vestry, Mr. Anton leaving at the same time.
To the E.litor of the"
Sir,—The I.llowinif is an exact copy of a notice issued by the Her. 11. Anton. St. llsrlishas Vestry, Nov. 12th, 1389. . . . . .
Dear Sir,-3 meeting of the Chung, Committee will be held intim above wistry, on Friday evening, Nov. 15th, at 7.30. .
• ..ss• Your attendance is earnestly requested. Yours faithfully, 6. ALLTON.

So far there is no committee formed, and Oli the parish- iiiners assembling they were informed it was a devotional meeting. and the Vicar summarily brought it to a close by having the light put nut. Continent is unnecessary. ONE WHO WAS THERE. Warrington, 15 Nov., 1889.
